entry.title: Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority [2026] FCA 1615
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

entry.title: ZKDP and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2505
entry.content:
ZKDP sought review of a delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa after a 7-year-6-month drug trafficking sentence. The Tribunal found he did not pass the character test but nevertheless set aside the refusal and substituted revocation after applying Direction No. 110. It weighed community protection against ties, rehabilitation, pending charges and other factors in a fact-specific decision.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), a mandatory cancellation may be revoked where the required representations have been made and the decision-maker is satisfied that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

Under s 501CA(4) of the Act, the Minister may revoke the original decision to cancel if the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation and the Minister is satisfied that the person passes the character test or there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

entry.title: Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1602
entry.content:
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.

Key holding: The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

The correct identification of the limits of the primary considerations referred to in Direction 110 did not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by Mr Roseingrave.

entry.title: Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1589
entry.content:
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.

Key holding: Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

entry.title: Phan and Australian Skills Quality Authority [2026] ARTA 2457
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed ASQA’s decision to cancel Mr Phan’s CPC31320 Certificate III in Wall and Floor Tiling, obtained through RPL from the deregistered RTO Kingsway. It found reasonable grounds that Kingsway did not provide or arrange the necessary RPL assessment and declined to exercise its discretion not to cancel. The reviewable decision was affirmed.

Key holding: Under s 56(1)(a) of the NVR Act, a VET qualification may be cancelled where the Tribunal is satisfied on reasonable grounds that the former RTO did not provide, or arrange for another person to provide, the assessment necessary for the person to achieve the required learning outcomes or competencies.

The Tribunal determines this matter under subsection 56(1)(a) of the NVR Act as it is satisfied on reasonable grounds that Kingsway did not provide, or arrange for another person to provide, the gap training or the assessment necessary for Mr Phan to achieve the learning outcomes or competencies required for the Qualification.

entry.title: Gates-Pilcher and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2500
entry.content:
This case concerned an application for Australian citizenship by descent by a New Zealand citizen with serious violent offending and non-disclosure of his criminal record. The Tribunal was not positively satisfied that he met the good character criterion and affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: For citizenship by descent under s 16(2)(c) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), the Tribunal must be positively satisfied that the applicant is of good character at the time of decision; if not, the application cannot be approved.

The Tribunal notes that the good character test does not require it to form an adverse view of the Applicant's character. Rather, it must be positively persuaded or positively satisfied that the Applicant is of good character.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1547
entry.content:
This was a judicial review of the Administrative Review Tribunal’s decision affirming non-revocation of Mr Dabea’s visa cancellation under s 501CA(4) after serious child sexual offences. Mr Dabea alleged the Tribunal failed to properly consider impediments if removed to Fiji and denied procedural fairness by sending post-hearing DFAT country information. The Federal Court dismissed the application.

Key holding: On judicial review, a tribunal’s reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, so a failure to evaluate a mandatory consideration is not readily inferred merely because the reasons are brief.

The task on judicial review is to read the reasons fairly and as a whole: see EGH19 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] HCA 33 at [68] (Gordon, Steward and Gleeson JJ).

entry.content:

The Tribunal found the offending serious and that community protection and expectations outweighed a low risk of reoffending and the applicant’s ties.

entry.title: Hoang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2396
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed the Minister’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Hoang’s Class BF Transitional (Permanent) visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although Mr Hoang had a substantial criminal record for repeat drug and weapons offending and failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4) and set aside the refusal.

Key holding: A residual risk of reoffending may be acceptable, and another reason to revoke may exist, where serious addiction-related offending is offset by sustained rehabilitation, family support and long residence.

The Applicant has, nonetheless, made significant progress in rehabilitation and has retained the support and trust of his immediate family who are an important element to his future success. I consider that the 'residual' risk of reoffending is acceptable despite the potentially serious consequences for the community, and Mr Hoang's length of residence from a young age must take into account.

entry.title: Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1531
entry.content:
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.

Key holding: A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

entry.title: YVXP v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1544
entry.content:
YVXP sought judicial review of the Administrative Review Tribunal’s decision affirming cancellation of his Class BB Subclass 155 Five Year Resident Return visa under s 501(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Federal Court found the Tribunal misapplied Direction No. 110 by treating cl 5.2 principles as modifying cl 8.5 expectations, misapplying cl 5.2(6), and failing to consider the six children’s best interests individually under cl 8.4(3). The Tribunal’s decision was quashed and remitted for redetermination.

Key holding: Where two or more affected children have differing interests, Direction No. 110 cl 8.4(3) requires the Tribunal to give individual consideration to each child’s best interests; collective consideration does not discharge that obligation.

Clause 8.4(3) mandates individual consideration of each of the children's interests, to the extent that their interests may differ, which did not occur in this case.

entry.title: Tran and Australian Skills Quality Authority [2026] ARTA 2300
entry.content:
Mr Tran sought review of ASQA’s decision to cancel his Certificate III in Carpentry, obtained via RPL from Kingsway, a deregistered RTO. Although the Tribunal found the s 56(1)(a) ground was established because Kingsway did not provide or arrange the necessary assessment, it exercised the discretion not to cancel in exceptional circumstances. The cancellation decision was set aside and the qualification is to be treated as a valid VET RPL qualification.

Key holding: Even when the s 56(1)(a) ground is established, the Tribunal may exercise the s 56(1) discretion not to cancel a VET qualification in exceptional circumstances, including clear lack of applicant fault, misleading RTO conduct, extensive genuine industry experience, and a public interest that does not require cancellation.

The Tribunal is satisfied that the discretion under subsection 56(1) of the NVR Act not to cancel the Qualification can be safely and appropriately exercised in the exceptional circumstances of this case. That discretion may be exercised consistent with the public interest, given that Mr Tran possesses the requisite training, skills and work experience to have been awarded the Qualification on an RPL basis.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), where an applicant fails the character test, the Tribunal may revoke mandatory cancellation if satisfied there is another reason, applying Direction no. 110.

entry.title: Daniel v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1480
entry.content:
Mr Daniel sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision refusing to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his Class TY Subclass 444 visa after he failed the character test due to a substantial criminal record. He alleged the Tribunal misconstrued the tolerance principle in Ministerial Direction 110 and reasoned illogically about reoffending, rehabilitation and weight. The Federal Court dismissed the application with costs.

Key holding: Paragraph 5.2(6) of Ministerial Direction 110 does not deem a higher tolerance and is not a mandatory consideration; it is a framework principle the Tribunal may consider.

First, principle (6) does not deem the Australian community to have a higher tolerance of criminal conduct on the part of those who have lived in Australia for most of their lives, nor indeed those who have lived in Australia from a very young age. As Kumar makes plain, the Tribunal is not required to have regard to it at all; it rises no higher than a consideration within the decision-making framework to which a Tribunal may have regard.

entry.title: Cristobal Fida v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1471
entry.content:
The applicant sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Working Holiday visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) due to character concerns. The Federal Court allowed the application, finding the Tribunal misapplied Direction 110 by assessing substantive visa eligibility rather than whether the duration and purpose of the intended stay affected risk of harm to the Australian community. The Tribunal decision was quashed and the matter remitted for determination according to law.

Key holding: Under Direction 110 [8.1.2(2)(c)], the Tribunal must consider whether and how the duration and purpose of an intended stay affect risk of harm to the Australian community, not whether the applicant satisfies substantive visa eligibility criteria.

The Tribunal erred by misapprehending the nature of the inquiry. It was required to consider, under [8.1.2(2)(c)] of Direction 110, how the duration and purpose of the intended stay affected the risk of harm to the Australian community, and misconstrued its task by considering the issue through the wrong lens (possible visa ineligibility).

entry.title: Upson and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2275
entry.content:
In Upson and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2275, a 31-year-old New Zealand citizen who has lived in Australia since infancy had his special category visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) after being sentenced to 7 years 6 months for serious drug offences. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, but the Administrative Review Tribunal set that decision aside and substituted revocation after finding “another reason” under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii).

Key holding: Under Direction no. 110, whether a non-citizen poses an “unacceptable risk” is a distinct evaluative conclusion reached by balancing the likelihood and potential harm of future offending, not merely the likelihood of re-offending.

The concept of 'risk', and whether it is 'unacceptable', under cl 8.1.2(1) of the Direction is not the same thing as the 'likelihood of the non-citizen engaging in further criminal or other serious conduct'.[25]

entry.title: Bekir Pty Ltd (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2393
entry.content:
In Bekir Pty Ltd (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2393, the sponsor sought review of a delegate’s decision to bar it for six months under s 140M of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), based on an alleged failure to ensure its sponsored employee worked as a Chef contrary to reg 2.86 of the Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth). The Tribunal found Mr Singh’s duties substantially aligned with ANZSCO Chef and no reg 2.86 breach, while a Fair Work Ombudsman NES contravention under reg 2.92(2) did not warrant any s 140M action. The Tribunal set aside the bar.

Key holding: Whether an employee performs the nominated occupation of Chef is assessed against ANZSCO duties, skills, qualifications and experience, not an additional delegate-imposed requirement of dish complexity.

Therefore, having proper regard to the ANZSCO guidance, a Chef is a Chef having regard to their skills, qualifications, experience and the performance of the associated duties.

entry.content:
This is a review of a refusal to grant a Student (Temporary) (Class TU) Subclass 500 visa. The delegate refused because the applicant, an Indian citizen, was not satisfied to be a genuine temporary entrant under cl 500.212. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: Refusal is upheld where the Tribunal is not satisfied, after considering Direction No 108 factors as a whole, that the applicant genuinely intends to stay in Australia temporarily under cl 500.212(a).

Overall having considered the criteria in Direction 108 and the relevant circumstances of the applicant, the Tribunal it is not satisfied that the applicant intends to stay in Australia temporarily. Accordingly, the applicant does not meet cl 500.212(a).

entry.title: Goro (Migration) [2024] AATA 3396
entry.content:
Ms Goro held a Subclass 500 (Student) visa. Her enrolments were cancelled in February 2022 and July 2022, leaving her unenrolled until the visa was cancelled on 6 September 2023. The Tribunal affirmed cancellation for breach of condition 8202(2)(a), finding no sufficient reason to exercise the cancellation discretion in her favour.

Key holding: A student visa holder’s failure to maintain enrolment in a full-time registered course breaches condition 8202 and enlivens the s 116(1)(b) cancellation ground, after which cancellation is a discretionary decision.

The issue in this case is whether the applicant, as the holder of a student visa, has breached condition 8202 of the Regulations. If so, the ground for cancellation is made out and the issue then becomes whether the visa should be cancelled pursuant to section 116(1) of the Act.
